senses: any object made of gold, such as a gold coin or a gold ring
la:noun:aurum.html:
aurum (Sab. ausum, Paul. ex Müll.; vulg. Lat., ōrum, ; cf. Ital. and Span. oro and Fr. or), i, n.
v. aes
.
Gold; as a mineral, v. sqq.: auri venas invenire,: venas auri sequi,; : aurum igni perspicere,: eruere terrā,: auri fodina,; ; ; ; Naev. ap. : ex auro vestis, (ap. ) et saep.— Provv.: montes auri polliceri,to promise mountains of gold,: carius auro,more precious than gold, (cf.: κρεισσονα χρυσοῦ, Aesch. Choëph. 372; χρυσοῦ χρυσότερα, Sapph. Fr. 122. Ellis).—
Meton.
Things made of gold, an ornament of gold, a golden vessel, utensil, etc.: Nec domus argento fulget nec auro renidet,gold plate,. So,
A golden goblet: et pleno se proluit auro,: Regales epulae mensis et Bacchus in auro Ponitur,: tibi non committitur aurum,; ; ; and in the hendiadys: pateris libamus et auro = pateris aureis,.—
A golden chain, buckle, clasp, necklace, jewelry: Oneratas veste atque auro,: Donec eum conjunx fatale poposcerit aurum,; .—
A gold ring: Ventilet aestivum digitis sudantibus aurum,.—
A golden bit: fulvum mandunt sub dentibus aurum,; .—
The golden fleece: auro Heros Aesonius potitur,.—
A golden hairband, κρωβύλος: crines nodantur in aurum, Serv.—
Esp. freq., gold as coined money: si quis illam invenerit Aulam onustam auri,: De Caelio vide, quaeso, ne quae lacuna sit in auro,: Aurum omnes victā jam pietate colunt,: quid non mortalia pectora cogis Auri sacra fames?; cf. ; so ; ; ; ; ; ; , 2, 179; ; et saep.—
The color or lustre of gold, the gleam or brightness of gold, : anguis cristis praesignis et auro (hendiadys, for cristis aureis),: saevo cum nox accenditur auro, (i. e. mala portendente splendore, Wagn.); so, fulgor auri, of the face,, ubi v. Ellis.—
The Golden Age: redeant in aurum Tempora priscum,: subiit argentea proles, Auro deterior,; .

la:verb:auro.html:
auro, āre, v. a.
aurum
,
to overlay with gold, to gild: a metallorum quoque nominibus solent nasci verba, ut ab auro auro, auras; ab aere aero, aeras, unde aeratus et auratus, etc., P.—As finite verb only in one (doubtful) example in .—But very freq. aurā-tus, a, um, P. a.
Furnished, overlaid, or ornamented with gold, gilded, gilt: auratus aries Colchorum, Enn. ap. : aurata metalla,metals rich in gold,: tecta,, and : tempora,covered with a golden helmet,: lacerti,: sinus, ornamented with a golden buckle, clasp, pin, etc., : vestes,. 448: amictus,: stolae, * : milites,with golden shields,—Comp.: auratior hostia,—
Of gold, golden: pellis,; : monilia,; cf.: regum auratis circumdata colla catenis,: lyra,; —
Gold-colored: gemma nunc sanguineis, nunc auratis guttis,.—Hence, subst.: aurāta, ae, f. (ōrāta, Paul. ex Fest. pp. 182 sq. Müll.; cf. aurum init.; Schneid. Gr. 1, p. 59), a fish, the gilt-bream: Sparus aurata, Linn.; . 18; 2, 28; ; .

la:noun:auriga.html:
aurīga, ae (aureax, Paul. ex Fest p. 8 Müll.), comm. (cf. P.) [aureaago], pr.,
he that handles the reins.
A charioteer, driver (syn.: agitator, agaso),; Hor C. 1, 15, 26; ; ; ; Vulg 3 Reg. 22, 34; ; al.—Also, a groom, hostler, .—In fem.: nec currus usquam videt aurigamque sororem,.—Also, one who contended in the chariot-race, a charioteer in the games of the circus (the four parties of whom were distinguished by the colors, Veneta, blue, Prasina, green, Alba, white, and Russea sive Russata, red; cf ; Gesn. ): auriga indoctus, Fragm. ap. (p. 328 Mos.); so ; ; ; .—
Transf.
As a constellation, the Wagoner, Gr. ̔Ηνιόχος, ; ; .—
Poet, a pilot, helmsman: aurigam video vela dedisse rati,.—
Trop., director, leader: velut auriga rectrixque membrorum anima,.

la:noun:auris.html:
auris (abl., aure, auri), is, f.
v. audio
.
Lit., the ear as the organ of hearing, while auricula is the external ear, τὸ οὖς, Enn. ap. ; ; ; ; ; v. antestor.—In comic style: Face, sis, vocivas aedīs aurium,make the chambers of your ears vacant,; cf. aedes.—Hence (usu. plur., aures): adhibere,to be attentive, to listen to,; : arrigere,; : erigere,; : admovere aurem,; : dare,to lend an ear, listen,; ; : dederet,: applicare,; : praebere aures, Liv 38, 52, 11; 40, 8, 3: praebuimus longis ambagibus aures,; ; ; 15, 465; and: praebere aurem (esp. in the signif., to incline the ears in order to hear, to listen to), ; ; ; ; ; ; so, inclinare aurem,; : auribus accipere,i. e. to hear,; ; ; ; ; : auribus percipite,; : te cupidā captat aure maritus,; so, auribus aëra captat,: auribus haurire,; : bibere aure,: obtundere,: tundere,: lacessere,: tergere,: allicere,: ferire,: implere, et saep.—Particular phrases: in or ad aurem, also in aure, dicere, admonere, etc., to say something in the ear, softly or in secret, to whisper in the ear: in aurem Pontius, Scipio, inquit, vide quid agas, ap. ; so ; ; : ut Voluptati ministrarent et eam tantum ad aurem admonerent,: in aure dictare, Juv 11, 59: aurem vellere, to pull, as an admonition: Cynthius aurem Vellit et admonuit,i. e. admonished, reminded,; so, pervellere,; : dare or servire auribus, to gratify the ears, to flatter, Treb. ap. ; : in

utramvis or in dextram aurem dormire, to sleep soundly, i. e. to be unconcerned, (cf. Menaud. ap. : ̓Επʼ ἀμφοτέραν ... μέλλει καθευδήσειν); ; : aures alicujus aperire (eccl. Lat., after the Heb.), to open one's ears, i. e. to restore his hearing, .—

Meton.
The hearing, so far as it judges of the euphony of a discourse: offendent aures, quarum est judicium superbissimum,; so Auct. ad : Atticorum aures teretes et religiosae,; so ; ; .—
Hearers, auditors: Cum tibi sol tepidus plures admoverit aures,.—*
Also, from its shape, the ear of a plough, the mould- or earthboard by which the furrow is widened and the earth turned back, ; cf. Voss ad h. 1.; Smith, Dict. Antiq., and .

la:noun:aura.html:
aura, ae (
gen. sing. aurāï, ; v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 11; also, auras, like familias, custodias, terras, etc.; Servius gives this in ; still all the MSS. give aurae, and so Rib.), f., = αὔρα [ΑΩ, αὔω, to blow].
The air, as in gentle motion, a gentle breeze, a breath of air (syn.: aër, ventus, spiritus): agitatus aër auram facit,: semper aër spiritu aliquo movetur; frequentius tamen auras quam ventos habet,: flatus, qui non aura, non procella, sed venti sunt,: et me... nunc omnes terrent aurae,now every breeze terrifies me,: Concutiat tenerum quaelibet aura,.— Hence,
Transf.
In gen., a breeze, a wind (even when violent): Et reserata viget genitabilis aura Favoni,; cf.: Aura parit flores tepidi fecunda Favoni. : omnes, Aspice, ventosi ceciderunt murmuris aurae,: aurae Vela vocant,: aura post meridiem,: aura tenuis,: lenis, ib. Job, 4, 16: petulans,: ignarae,brutish,, ubi v. Ellis: rapida,: stridens,: violentior,: aurae flatus,: omnes eos tollet aura, et saep.—Also breath: flammas exsuscitat aura,.—
Trop.: dum flavit velis aura secunda meis, while a favorable breeze breathed on my sails, i. e. so long as I was in prosperity, : totam opinionem parva non numquam commutat aura rumoris,: tenuis famae aura,: quem neque periculi tempestas neque honoris aura potuit umquam de suo cursu aut spe aut metu demovere,: levi aurā spei objectā,: sperat sibi auram posse aliquam adflari in hoc crimine voluntatis defensionisque eorum, quibus, etc.,token of favor,: nescius aurae (sc. amoris) Fallacis,: incerta Cupidinis aura,.—Hence freq. aura popularis, the popular breeze, popular favor, ; ; ; ; (cf.: ventus popularis,); so, aura favoris popularis,.—Also in plur.: nimium gaudens popularibus auris,; and absol.: adliciendo ad se plebem jam aurā non consilio ferri,.—
The air (mostly poet. and plur.): cum Nubila portabunt venti transversa per auras,: Tenvis enim quaedam moribundos deserit aura,: Aurarumque leves animae calidique vapores,: (anima) discedit in auras,; et saep.—Hence, aurae aëris or aëriae aurae freq. in Lucr.: (res) Aëris in teneras possint proferrier auras, 1, 207; 1, 783; 1, 801; 1, 803; 1, 1087; 2, 203; 3, 456; 3, 570; 3, 591; 4, 693: liquidissimus aether Atque levissimus aërias super influit auras,; ; : Nulla nec aërias volucris perlabitur auras,: Qui tamen aërias telum contorsit in auras,.—
Esp., the vital air: Vivit et aetherias vitalīs suscipit auras,breathes a breath of ethereal air,; imitated by Verg.: haud invisus caelestibus auras Vitales carpis, A. 1, 387: vesci vitalibus auris, i. e. vivere,; imitated by Verg., A. 1, 546, and 3, 339; so, haurire auram communem,: captare naribus auras,to snuff the air,.—Trop.: libertatis auram captare, to catch at the air of freedom, i. e. to seize upon any hope of liberty, Liv 3, 37, 1.—
Meton.
The upper air, Heaven, on high: assurgere in auras,; so : dum se laetus ad auras Palmes agit,: ad auras Aetherias tendit,; so : stat ferrea turris ad auras, poet. for ad alta, rises high, : Sorbet in abruptum fluctus, rursusque sub auras Erigit alternos, ; 7, 466; 2, 759; 5, 427 al.; cf. Wagner, Quaest. .—
In opp. to the lower world, the upper world (cf. aether, I. B. 3.): Eurydice superas veniebat ad auras,; so : Ortygiam, quae me superas eduxit prima sub auras,; (cf. : ad superos); so of childbirth: pondus in auras expulit,.—In gen. for publicity, daylight: ferre sub auras,i. e. to make known,: reddere ad auras,to restore,: fugere auras, to seclude or hide one's self, .—
Transf. to other atmospheric objects which exert an influence on bodies, as light, heat, sound, vapor, etc.
A bright light, a gleam, glittering (cf. φάεος ἀϋτμή, Callim. Hymn. Dian. 117): discolor unde auri per ramos aura refulsit, (splendor auri, Serv.).—
The warmth of sunlight: solis calidior visa est aura, Varr. ap. .—
Sound, tone, voice, echo: Si modo damnatum revocaverit aura puellae,: at illi Nomen ab extremis fontibus aura refert,.—
Vapor, mist, odor, exhalation: inolentis olivi Naturam, nullam quae mittat naribus auram,: at illi Dulcis compositis spiravit crinibus aura,a sweet odor exhaled,; so ; ; cf. Heins. ad : si tantum notas odor attulit auras,: pingues ab ovilibus aurae,.

aurĕus, a, um, adj.
id.

Lit.
Of gold, golden (syn.: aureolus, auratus, aurifer): patera, and 263: vasa,; : torulus,: imber,: funis,: torques. : simulacra,: mala Hesperidum,: aurea mala,: pelles,: corona (a gift for distinction in war),; ; ; : corona,: candelabra,: nummus, and absol.: aurĕus, i, m., the standard gold coin of Rome, a gold piece (first struck in the second Punic war), of the value of 25 denarii or 100 sestertii (weighing about 120 grains, and being about equal to £1, 1s. 1d. or $5.10), : si (tibi) contigit aureus unus. ; fully, aureus nummus,; ; ; ; ; —Of the Hebrew shekels (eccl. Lat.), ; ; 9, 16.—Poet.: vis aurea tinxit Flumen,i. e. the power of changing every thing to gold,.—
Furnished with gold, wrought, interwoven, or ornamented with gold, gilded: victimam auream polcram immolabat,i. e. with gilded horns, (cf. Hom. Od. 3, 426): sella,, and : cingula,: Capitolia,. templa, : cuspis,: Pactolus,whose waters flowed with gold,; cf: Lucr 5, 911 sq.—
Of the color of gold, glittering like gold, golden: liquidi color aureus ignis,: Barba erat incipiens, barbae color aureus,; ; ; : lumina solis,; so, aurea Phoebe,; : luna,; : aureus sol,; ; so : sidera, Verg A. 2, 488; 11, 832: caesaries,golden locks,: coma,, and : aurea mala,, and 8, 52: Aurea pavonum ridenti imbuta lepore Saecla, the golden species of peacock, full of laughing beauty, Lucr 2, 502.—
Trop., of physical and mental excellences or attractions, golden, beautiful, splendid: aurea Venus,; Ov M. 10, 277; 15, 761: Amor,: Copia,: Aurea Phoebi porticus,: litus,: aether,: medicamentum,: dicta, vita, and 13: mores,: Qui nunc te fruitur credulus aureā,: tua mater Me movet atque iras aurea vincit anus,: mediocritas,the golden mean,: aetas,the golden age,: tempus,.—Hence, Virgo = Astraea, .

la:other:Aurelius.html:
Aurēlĭus (Ausēlĭus, Paul. ex Müll.), a, um, adj.
A Roman nomen, e. g. M. Aurelius Antoninus, L. Aurelius Cotta; hence,
Esp.
Aurelia Via, the Aurelian Way, made by a certain Aurelius, otherwise unknown; it consisted of two parts: VETVS ET NOVA,; the former ran from the Porta Janiculensis (now Porta di S. Pancrazio) of the northern coast to Pisa, later to Arelate; the latter was a small branch which led from the Porta Aurelia (now Castel S. Angelo) four thousand paces, to the former The via vetus Cicero mentions in ; Phil. 12, 9.—
Aurelia lex.
Judiciaria, of the prœtor L. Aurelius Cotta (A. U. C. 684), acc. to which the Senatores, Equites, and Tribuni aerarii were invested with judicial power, ; ; .—
De ambitu,

of unknown origin, —

Forum Aurelium, a town in Etruria, on the Via Aurelia, near the present village Castellacio, ; cf. Mann. Ital. I. p. 370.—
Aurelium tribunal, in the forum, of unknown origin (perh, made by L. Aurelius Cotta), ; ; also called Gradus Aurelii,; .—
Sextus Aurelius Victor, a Roman historian of the fourth century; cf. Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 342 sq.; Teuffel, Rom. Lit. § 408.

la:noun:aurora.html:
aurōra, ae, f.
acc. to Curtius, a reduplicated form for ausosa, from Sanscr. ush, to burn; cf. αὔως = ἠώς, dawn; ἥλιος, the sun; and Etrusc. Usil, the god of the sun; but its idea of brightness, splendor, easily connects it with the same group as aurum; v. aes
.
The dawn, daybreak, morning (mostly poet.): est autem aurora diei clarescentis exordium et primus splendor aëris, quae Graece ἠώς dicitur, : usque ab aurorā ad hoc quod diei est,: Nec nox ulla diem neque noctem aurora secutast,; 4, 538; 4, 711; 5, 657; : ad primam auroram,; .—
Personified, the goddess of the morning, Gr. ̓Ηώς, daughter of Hyperion (hence Hyperionis, ), wife of Tithonus (hence Tithonia conjunx, , and Tithonia, ), and mother of Memnon, : Aurora novo cum spargit lumine terras,; imitated by Verg. l.l.; 9, 459: Iamque rubescebat stellis Aurora fugatis,; 6, 535; 7, 26: Proxima prospiciet Tithono Aurora relicto,; ; she robbed Procris of her husband, Cephalus,; but gave him back,.—
Meton., the East, the Orient: ab Aurorae populis et litore rubro,: Eurus ad Auroram Nabataeaque regna recessit,: quae (terrae) sunt a Gadibus usque Auroram et Gangen,; cf. ; so ; ; also,the people of the East,; ; ; .
